input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Here’s how you could explain it to a 5-year-old:

When someone gets a new heart, kidney, or another organ from someone else, that new organ is made up of the other person’s cells. At first, most of those donor cells stay the same. But over time, some of the host’s own body cells might move into the new organ, and some of the donor’s cells might not last forever. However, the new organ will mostly stay made up of the donor’s cells for a long, long time—maybe even for the rest of the person’s life. But it’s not exactly the same as if it was grown inside their own body.
